knowledgeAnswers.rationale: Colourfastness is tested by transfer onto a white cloth from an inconspicuous area, using the planned product. Looking at or smelling the product is not a test.
Colour transfer means the product is not suitable for that fabric and colour. The product is refused and a tested conservative alternative or referral is offered.
Leather and vinyl have finishes or coatings that can react to products that suit textiles, so they are approached differently. This is general practice.
Velvet and other pile fabrics need a gentle, pile-aware method, tested first. Hard brushing can crush or mark the pile.

practicalCriteria: Identifies four upholstery sample fabrics from the label, feel, weave or knit and pile, or records any one as unidentified and treats it as sensitive.
Carries out a colourfastness test on a sample fabric on an inconspicuous area, using a white cloth, and reads the result after drying.
Refuses a simulated treatment after the test shows colour transfer, and records the refusal and the alternative offered.
Uses a gentle, pile-aware method on a simulated pile fabric, with no hard brushing, after a test.
passRule: Fabrics identified or recorded as unidentified, colourfastness test completed and read after drying, failed treatment refused with the record complete, and pile handled gently. Observed by an assessor. A knowledge check result is not a practical pass.
evidenceRequired: Photographs of the test area and the white cloth, taken with permission
stopWorkCriteria: Hard brushing on a pile fabric
A solvent used on an unidentified leather or vinyl finish
